# From linked data to research-ready data {#sec-pipeline}

```{r}
source("R/book.R")
sc <- read_pipeline("outputs", "quality", "scope_counts.csv")
hs <- read_pipeline("outputs", "quality", "harmonised_sources.csv")
n_in <- sc$n_vehicles[sc$measure == "input_rows"]
n_scope <- sc$n_vehicles[sc$measure == "in_scope"]
```

The linked table from the linkage stage (@sec-sources-linkage) is accurate to
its sources, but not yet easy to analyse. The same make is spelt dozens of
ways, attributes are missing for many vehicles, and some DVLA records belong to
another vehicle. The pipeline,
[MOT-pipline](https://github.com/CARS-Project/MOT-pipline), cleans and enhances
the table and produces the published outputs. This chapter summarises what it
does; the full method, with every rule and count, is in the pipeline's
[Methodology](../reports/methodology.md), included as an appendix.

## Principles

Four principles run through the pipeline, and they shape how the data should be
used:

1. **Supplied values are never overwritten.** Cleaned, harmonised or filled
   values go in new columns next to the originals. `fuel_DVSA` is the fuel as
   DVSA supplied it; `fuel` is the harmonised fuel.
2. **Every inferred value records its source.** Columns ending `_src`,
   `_method` and `_check` say how each value was reached, so you can always
   separate what was recorded from what was inferred.
3. **Weak evidence is flagged, not acted on.** A value is changed only when the
   vehicle's own records disagree and a second source settles it.
4. **Results are reproducible.** Every step is a rule (no language model or
   random element is used), and rebuilding from the same input gives the same
   output.

## The stages

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[Linked and annualised<br/>vehicle table] --> B[1. Core table<br/>scope, dates, yearly status]
    B --> C[2. Make and model<br/>matched to DfT names]
    T[DfT vehicle licensing<br/>statistics] --> C
    A --> M[3a. DVSA-DVLA<br/>record check]
    C --> F[3b. Fuel and engine checks]
    M --> F
    F --> D[3c. Fill gaps from<br/>similar vehicles]
    D --> E[4. Vehicle table<br/>vehicles_enhanced.parquet]
    E --> G[Churn tables]
    E --> H[Mileage and fleet<br/>profile tables]
    E --> I[Quality reports]
```

### 1. Core table: which vehicles, and their dates

The input holds `r fmt_n(n_in)` vehicles, many of which left the roads long
before 2005. The pipeline keeps every vehicle with evidence that it existed
from 2005 onwards: a recorded mileage or postcode area in any year, a birth
date from 2005, or DVLA activity (tax, V5C, MOT expiry or first registration)
since 2005. That leaves **`r fmt_n(n_scope)` vehicles**. The `scope_*` columns
record which evidence each vehicle has.

It also sets each vehicle's `birth_date` (the earliest of its first-use,
registration and manufacture dates) and `first_use_date`, and fills the blank
years of `pca_YYYY` with the statuses `unborn`, `unknown` and `dead`
(@sec-lifecycle).

### 2. Make and model

DVSA records make and model as free text, entered at the test station. "FORD
FIESTA ZETEC CLIMATE", "Fiesta" and "MOMDEO" all occur. The pipeline matches
each distinct make and model to the names DfT uses in its vehicle licensing
statistics, through a sequence of rules (exact match, generic name, prefix,
words, spelling fixes) that each record how they matched:

| Column | Example |
|---|---|
| `make_final` | `FORD` |
| `model_final` | `FIESTA` (DfT's *generic model*) |
| `derivative_final` | `ZETEC CLIMATE`: the rest of the model text |
| `dft_genmodel` | `FORD FIESTA`, for joining to DfT tables |
| `make_method`, `model_method`, `model_confidence` | How the match was made, and how sure it is |

Using DfT's names means CARS results can be joined to and compared with the
official statistics. The DfT scheme is sometimes coarser than a buyer would
use (DfT's DISCOVERY includes the Discovery Sport), and the derivative keeps the
detail. The match also gives each vehicle a DfT `body_type`
(@sec-vehicle-types).

### 3. Checking and harmonising attributes

Eight attributes are *harmonised*: given one best value per vehicle from the
DVSA record, the DVLA record and, where both are missing, similar vehicles.
They are `fuel`, `engine_cc`, `co2`, `euro_status`, `type_approval`,
`revenue_weight`, `wheelplan` and `test_class`.

- **Is the DVLA record the same vehicle?** The make, year and engine size of
  the DVSA and DVLA records are compared. Where two or more disagree
  (`dvla_match = 'different'`), the DVLA record is taken to describe another
  vehicle and none of its values is used.
- **Fuel** is taken from the records and never filled from other vehicles.
  DVLA's fuel is used where DVSA says "Other", or where DVSA says Electric for
  a vehicle that has an engine. Plug-in hybrids are identified from DfT's
  records for the model (@sec-fuels-emissions). `fuel_check` compares each
  vehicle's fuel with others of its make and model, and flags rare fuels.
- **Engine size** is 0 for electric vehicles.
- **Gaps** in the other attributes are filled with the most common value among
  vehicles of the same make, model, birth year and fuel (and engine size where
  known). Values are never borrowed across fuels.
- **Euro status** that is still missing is assumed from the standard
  compulsory when the vehicle was made (@sec-fuels-emissions).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-harmonised
#| tbl-cap: "Where the harmonised attributes come from: share of vehicles in the vehicle table."
grp <- list(
  "Recorded" = c("dvsa", "dvla"),
  "Rule (no engine, DfT, model check, Euro schedule)" =
    c("no_engine", "dft", "model", "euro_schedule"),
  "From similar vehicles" = c("variant", "model_year_fuel", "model_fuel"),
  "Missing" = "missing"
)
tot <- rowSums(hs[, -1])
tab <- data.frame(Attribute = hs$attribute)
for (g in names(grp)) {
  tab[[g]] <- fmt_pct(rowSums(hs[, grp[[g]], drop = FALSE]) / tot)
}
kable(tab, align = c("l", rep("r", 4)))
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Recorded values only"}
To check that a result does not depend on filled values, repeat it using
only recorded ones: filter on `co2_src = 'dvla'`, `euro_status_src = 'dvla'`,
`engine_cc_src IN ('dvsa', 'dvla')` and so on, or use the supplied columns
(`co2Emissions_DVLA`, `euroStatus_DVLA`). @sec-examples-code has an example.
:::

### 4. Number plates and derived fields

The registration number is decoded to its format, issue period and issuing
office, and flagged where it does not match the vehicle's age
(@sec-number-plates). Simplified groupings such as `fuel_simple` and
`euro_standard` are added.

Each car is also linked to the RACF car fleet, DfT's car fleet by model, year
of first use and fuel enriched with each model's SMMT segment and its mass,
dimensions, CO~2~, energy use and electric range from the EU type-approval
and Dutch RDW registers. The `racf_` columns give the fleet-weighted average
of these for the car's model, not measurements of the car itself
(@sec-dd-racf).

### Outputs

The result is the vehicle table, `vehicles_enhanced.parquet`, with its data
dictionary (@sec-vehicle-table). From it the pipeline builds the aggregate
tables (@sec-aggregate-tables) and a set of reports that document them,
included in this book as appendices.

## Validation

The pipeline has unit tests for every rule, a set of cross-checks run on every
build that compare published numbers that must agree, comparisons with DfT's
statistics (@sec-data-quality), and a record of an end-to-end audit. See the
[MOT-pipline repository](https://github.com/CARS-Project/MOT-pipline) for
details.
